feedback: For a mis-sort crossing the rules: re-pair each quantity with its configuration — in series the current is the same everywhere and the supply voltage is shared, so component voltages add to the supply; in parallel each branch gets the full supply voltage and branch currents add where they meet.
For 'adding a parallel branch reduces total current': it increases it, because total resistance drops with more routes.
For 'parallel bulbs are dimmer': each branch sees the full supply, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (ideal cell).
activities.intendedInsight: The rules and their practical consequences can be stated precisely and matched to the correct configuration, consolidating the contrast learned by building.
learnerActions: Sort statements into SERIES vs PARALLEL columns: 'current same everywhere', 'voltages across components add to the supply', 'each branch gets the full supply voltage', 'branch currents add where they meet'.
Predict the brightness of the first bulb when a second bulb is added in series, then when added in parallel.
Answer 'why is household wiring parallel?' and justify by a consequence (full voltage to each device, independent switching, one failing leaves others working).
Predict what happens to the total current when a parallel branch is added.
Rank circuits by total resistance as series components are added vs as parallel branches are added.
activities.title: Sort and predict: series vs parallel rules

feedback: If a learner picks series for the house 'to save wire': point to the consequence — shared voltage means dimmer devices and one failure breaks the whole loop.
If a learner cannot justify parallel: prompt them to trace what happens to each other device when one branch is removed.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a configuration for a real purpose forces the learner to reason from the rules to consequences, reinforcing why parallel is standard for independent, full-brightness, fault-tolerant devices.
learnerActions: Take on real design problems with an electrician persona: how to wire old-style fairy lights vs a house lighting circuit.

Argue, for each case, whether series or parallel is appropriate and give the consequence-based reason (does one failing kill the rest? does each device get full voltage? can each be switched independently?).
Explain why a house is NOT wired in series by describing what would go wrong if one lamp failed.
Contrast old series fairy-lights (one blows, all go out) with parallel wiring.
activities.title: Electrician's design problem: series or parallel?
